title: Ten Years of Listening to Black Holes Spin
hook: A decade after the first gravitational-wave detection, 100+ events let astronomers read black holes' spins — and spin turns out to reveal how the pairs were born.
key_points: Since 2015, gravitational-wave detectors have logged over a hundred confirmed black-hole mergers.
Each waveform carries an imprint of how fast and which way the black holes spin.
Different formation channels predict distinct spin signatures across the population.
Isolated binaries, dense star clusters, and AGN disks each leave their own fingerprint.
Spin patterns — and how they correlate with mass and distance — help decode where black hole pairs come from.
content_html: When LIGO caught the first gravitational waves in 2015, it opened a brand-new way to study black holes: by the spacetime ripples they shed when they merge. A decade on, the catalog has grown past a hundred confirmed events — enough to do statistics, not just spot individual collisions.
extra_html: In this review, Sylvia Biscoveanu surveys what that decade has taught us about one subtle but powerful property: black hole spin. A spinning black hole leaves a faint imprint on the gravitational waveform, encoding both how fast it rotates and how its spin axis is tilted. That matters because different birth stories predict different spins. Black holes that formed as an isolated pair of stars should spin differently from those that paired up by chance in a dense cluster, or inside the gas disk around a giant galaxy's central black hole. By measuring spins across the whole population — and how they correlate with mass and cosmic distance — astronomers are beginning to read off where these black hole pairs come from, with sharper answers expected as detectors grow more sensitive.

related.hook: When black holes collide, they shake the fabric of spacetime itself, sending out ripples that stretch and squeeze everything they pass — by less than the width of a proton.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.hook: When a giant star dies, its core collapses and its outer layers blast away in a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy — leaving behind something extraordinary.

related.hook: The latest gravitational-wave catalog leaps to 390 confirmed detections — including the clearest signal ever caught and evidence some black holes are built from earlier mergers.

flashcards.prompt: Why are black hole spins such a useful clue for astronomers?
flashcards.back_html: Different formation channels predict different spin magnitudes and orientations, so the population's spin pattern acts as a tracer of how black hole binaries form and evolve.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is one of the binary black hole formation channels the review discusses?

choices.text: Dynamical formation in dense star clusters
Direct condensation out of the cosmic microwave background
Spontaneous creation in the vacuum of empty space

flashcards.explanation_html: The review covers channels such as isolated binary evolution, dynamical formation in clusters, formation in AGN disks, and hierarchical triples — each leaving a distinct spin signature.
